lesson.intuition: An estimate trades detail for a useful scale or a guaranteed bound. Rounding to the nearest ten groups numbers into ten-wide neighborhoods; it does not erase the difference between an approximate answer and an exact one. Compatible numbers make mental arithmetic easier. For a budget or capacity decision, a deliberate upper bound can be safer than nearest rounding. The direction of each rounding step matters, and errors can accumulate across many items.

lesson.intuition: A direct proportion says one quantity is a constant multiple of another: y=kx. Every admissible nonzero input gives the same ratio y/x, and the graph passes through the origin. An inverse relationship has a constant product instead, so doubling one quantity halves the other when the model assumptions hold.

lesson.intuition: An equation is a balance between two expressions. Solving means finding every admissible value that makes it true. Adding the same quantity to both sides, or multiplying both by the same nonzero number, preserves equality and can be undone. These reversible operations isolate an unknown. Division by zero is unavailable, and some equations have no solution or every value as a solution. Substitution in the original equation checks both the arithmetic and the original restrictions.

lesson.intuition: An inequality describes an ordered range of possibilities rather than one required value. A strict sign excludes its boundary; ≤ or ≥ includes it. lesson.intuition: A linear system can be represented by an augmented matrix. Swapping rows, multiplying a row by a nonzero scalar and adding a multiple of one row to another preserve its solution set. lesson.intuition: An algorithm is a precise procedure with inputs, outputs and conditions. Correctness requires that its result meets the specification; termination requires that it finishes for permitted inputs. A loop invariant holds initially, survives each iteration and helps prove the postcondition at exit. Complexity counts work as input size grows under an explicit cost model. Big-O is an eventual upper bound, not an exact running time or a guarantee that a procedure is correct.
